stimulus:
A Fresnel lens looks like a dinner plate that gave up being thick. Augustin Fresnel noticed that only the surface of a lens bends light; the glass in the middle just sits there being heavy. So he sliced the curve into concentric rings and threw the bulk away. Suddenly a lens taller than a person could be built from prisms stacked like a beehive, and a lamp's glow could reach twenty miles. Funny that the same trick shows up in overhead projectors, car taillights, and those flimsy plastic magnifiers tucked in wallets.

The rotation is the part I like. The beam isn't a pulse at all; the lens just sweeps a steady beam past you, and your eye turns it into a flash. Each lighthouse has its own rhythm, two long, one short, a pause, so sailors can identify it like a name. Characters in the dark, written in time rather than ink.

The lens floated on a bath of liquid mercury so a clockwork weight could spin tons of glass with a nudge. Keepers wound it by hand, trimmed wicks, polished brass. Mercury fumes are a whole other story. Then automation arrived, LEDs and GPS, and the keepers left. Meanwhile, the lenses are sold at auction, sitting in museum lobbies, still quietly bending nothing at all.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Rhythm-decoding: AP-1 dynamics as a temporal code
ideas.description: Like a lighthouse's long-short pattern identifying it, drive cells with optogenetic or chemically-gated ERK/JNK pulses of varied frequency and duration, and live-image FOS/JUN reporters. Then test whether pulse pattern (not just total dose) determines distinct downstream chromatin states and gene programs that persist after stimulation stops.

ideas.title: Chromatin-accessibility memory after transient stimulation
ideas.description: Stimulate cells once, wash out, and perform ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN, FOSL) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at days 0, 1, 7, and 14 compared with naive cells. Persistent AP-1-bound, accessible 'primed' enhancers that give faster or stronger re-induction on second stimulation would indicate memory.

ideas.title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance (the 'bulk vs. surface' test)
ideas.description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the first stimulus or only after the memory is established. If depleting during priming abolishes later re-response but depleting afterward doesn't, AP-1 is needed to write the memory; if later depletion also erases it, AP-1 maintains it.

ideas.title: Single-cell prime-and-rechallenge with lineage tracing
ideas.description: Prime cells, let them divide, and perform single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with barcoded lineage tracking to see whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and response magnitude to a second challenge. Heritable clonal concordance of response, correlated with AP-1 occupancy, demonstrates mitotically stable memory rather than transient signaling.

ideas.title: Targeted enhancer perturbation and sufficiency test
ideas.description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation to silence or edit AP-1 binding sites at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 (dCas9-FOS/JUN) to naive loci. Measure whether the edits eliminate or create faster re-induction of the nearby gene, testing necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding for locus-specific memory.
